title: Studying medicine abroad and coming home to practise in Denmark
intro: Every year a group of Danish students who do not get a place on medicin at KU, AU, SDU or AAU go and study medicine in English somewhere else in Europe. Poland, Hungary and Czechia are the three countries that take the most of them. It is a real route and it works, but it is expensive and there is one legal detail that decides whether your degree lets you work as a doctor in Denmark. This page explains how entry works, what it costs, and exactly what you have to check before you sign anything.

sections.heading: Why this route exists
sections.body:
Danish medicine places are rationed. If you do not get in, the options are to re-apply, to do something else, or to pay for an English-taught medical degree abroad. Central European universities have run English-language medical programmes for decades, originally for American and Scandinavian students, and they are set up for exactly this. The teaching is in English for the whole degree. The patients are not, so you learn the local language alongside it for the clinical years.

This is a six-year undergraduate-entry degree, the same shape as the Danish one. You start straight after the IB. There is no separate pre-med.
bullets: Entry is by entrance exam and interview, not by a Danish grade-point average, so a strong IB student who missed the Danish cut-off is competitive.
You graduate with the country's ordinary national medical degree, the same one local students get. That is what makes EU recognition possible.
Clinical years are taught in English but you will need working Polish, Hungarian or Czech to talk to patients. Every one of these universities teaches it as a compulsory subject.
It is self-funded. There is no free English-taught medicine anywhere in this group of countries.

sections.heading: How entry actually works
sections.body:
You apply directly to each university, not through a central portal, and you can apply to several. Most run rolling admission from autumn through to summer, with places filling as they go, so applying early genuinely helps.

The selection is almost always an entrance examination in biology and chemistry, sometimes with physics or maths, sometimes followed by an interview. Several universities run their exam online or at exam centres outside the country, which means you can sit it without travelling. A few will exempt you from part of the exam on the strength of strong HL Biology and HL Chemistry grades, but you cannot assume that: check the specific programme.

Because you finish the IB in late May and results come out on 5-6 July, you will usually be admitted conditionally on your predicted grades and confirm with the final diploma. Ask the admissions office to put that in writing.
bullets: Take HL Biology and HL Chemistry if medicine abroad is even a maybe. Almost every entrance exam is built on that content.
Apply to more than one university. These are separate applications with separate fees and separate exams.
Deadlines and exam dates for autumn 2027 entry will mostly be published during autumn 2026. Check each university's own page rather than trusting a recruitment agency.
Ignore agencies that charge you a placement fee. You can apply to all of these directly, and the university's own admissions office will answer your questions for free.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body:
Tuition is the big number and it is paid every year for six years. Add living costs on top. See the Poland, Czechia and Hungary country pages on this site for the specific per-university figures and the academic year each one belongs to.

Danish SU and the Danish state student loan (SU-lan) can often be taken abroad for a full degree, and there is a separate scheme for tuition support. That is decided by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen in Denmark, not by the university abroad, and you have to apply for it yourself. Do that early, because it changes whether the whole plan is affordable.
bullets: Budget for six years of tuition, not one. Multiply before you decide.
Tuition at these programmes is normally the same for EU and non-EU students, because the fee is attached to the English-language programme rather than to your nationality.
Living costs in Poland, Czechia and Hungary are well below Danish levels, which offsets part of the tuition.
Check the Danish SU rules for udlandsstipendium and SU abroad before you commit. This is a Danish decision made in Denmark.

sections.heading: The part that decides everything: Danish authorisation
sections.body:
A medical degree is not the same thing as a licence to work as a doctor. In Denmark the licence is called autorisation, and the right to work without supervision is called tilladelse til selvstaendigt virke. Both are granted by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed.

The good news is that EU law is on your side. Under Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications, a medical qualification listed in Annex V point 5.1.1 is recognised automatically across the EU. Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed states plainly that you can get Danish authorisation and permission to practise independently if you are a citizen of an EU/EEA country or Switzerland and hold a medical degree from an EU/EEA country or Switzerland. Denmark does not make you repeat the Danish klinisk basisuddannelse in that case, and it does not make you sit a Danish medical exam.

The authority also says that automatic recognition depends on the education, not on the passport: someone who is not an EU citizen but who trained as a doctor in the EU/EEA may still be recognised under the automatic-recognition principles.
bullets: Applying for the authorisation itself is free. The permission to practise independently costs DKK 3,689.
The stated processing target is three months from a complete application, with priority given to applicants who already have a Danish job offer.

You need a certificate of conformity from the health authority of the country where you studied, confirming the training met the Directive's minimum requirements, plus a certificate of current professional status less than three months old.
Automatic recognition covers doctors, dentists, midwives and nurses. It rests on Directive 2005/36/EC and Danish executive order no. 49 of 13 January 2010.

sections.heading: The Poland trap: the diploma alone is not enough
sections.body:
This is the single most important thing on this page and it is the thing recruitment agencies do not tell you.

Annex V of the Directive lists, for each country, the qualification that gets automatic recognition and any certificates that must accompany it. For Czechia, Hungary and Estonia, the medical diploma stands alone: no accompanying certificate is listed. For Poland it does not. The Polish entry requires the diploma plus the certificate of the state final medical examination, the Lekarski Egzamin Koncowy (LEK), and Poland's own medical chamber says the certificate of completed postgraduate internship, staz podyplomowy, is also part of what accompanies the Polish diploma.

The Naczelna Izba Lekarska, the Polish chamber of physicians, puts it bluntly: it can only certify full Polish qualifications for EU recognition if you have both the LEK and a recognised postgraduate internship. If you have neither, what you can get instead is an Article 23 or 27 certificate of conformity, and the chamber says that certificate does not confirm that a graduate of a Polish university has obtained full qualifications to practise the profession in Poland.

In plain terms: if you graduate in Poland, come straight home and skip the LEK and the internship, you are not in the automatic-recognition track. You can still work towards Danish authorisation, but you are on a slower and less certain path.
bullets: The Polish postgraduate internship normally runs 13 months and is conducted in Polish, and it is paid.

Some Polish universities offer a shorter six-month internship taught in English, which you pay for, and which then has to be recognised by the Polish Ministry of Health as equivalent to the Polish one.

Some destination countries let you skip the Polish staz and do their own supervised year instead. Whether Denmark accepts a given arrangement is a question for Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed, and you should ask them in writing before you take the job.
Ask any Polish university you apply to, in writing: what exactly will I hold on graduation day, and what more do I need for Annex V recognition?

sections.heading: If automatic recognition does not apply to you
sections.body:
Denmark has a fallback for exactly this situation. The regional postgraduate training secretariats run what they call a KBU-lignende forlob, a KBU-like programme, for doctors trained inside the EU, EEA and the Nordic countries who have not been granted automatic authorisation. Doctors trained outside the EU/EEA go through a longer route of evalueringsansaettelser, evaluation posts of at least two times six months.

So the fallback exists, but it costs you time and it depends on getting a post. It is much better to graduate with the full set of documents than to arrive home and negotiate.
bullets: KBU itself is two six-month posts, one in a hospital and one usually in general practice or psychiatry, and Danish graduates must register for it within two years of finishing their degree.
A Dane with an EU medical degree that qualifies for automatic recognition does not have to go through KBU to get permission to practise independently.
Rules and fees change. The Danish authorisation fee structure was reworked on 1 July 2024, and restrictions introduced since then have been aimed at non-EU/EEA educations, not EU ones.
If anything about your case is unusual, write to Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed and get the answer in writing before you enrol, not after you graduate.

sections.heading: Language, and the bit nobody warns you about
sections.body:
There is no formal Danish language test imposed by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed on doctors trained inside the EU. Under EU law the authority has to issue the authorisation on the basis of the qualification. Danish language competence is treated as the employer's responsibility, and Danish hospitals do check it.

That cuts both ways. Legally you are fine. Practically, a Danish hospital will not hire you if your clinical Danish is weak, and if you have spent six years working in Polish, Hungarian or Czech, your Danish medical vocabulary will be thin. Danish doctors' organisations have publicly argued for a formal language test for EU-trained doctors; that has not become law, but it tells you what employers think.

Keep your Danish alive while you are away. Do Danish-language clinical placements or summer jobs in Denmark if you can.
bullets: No Danish language exam is required for authorisation if you trained in the EU/EEA.
The employer is responsible for making sure your Danish is good enough for the job.
You will also need the local language for clinical years abroad, so you are learning two languages at once.
This is a live political debate in Denmark, so check whether the rule has changed by the time you graduate.

sections.heading: A checklist before you commit
sections.body: Print this and work through it with the admissions office of every university you are seriously considering. Get answers in writing.
bullets: Is the degree I will receive the same national medical degree that local students receive, and is it the one listed in Annex V point 5.1.1 of Directive 2005/36/EC?
Will the national health authority issue me a certificate of conformity confirming the training meets the Directive's minimum requirements?
In this country, does the diploma alone carry recognition, or do I also need a state exam and a postgraduate internship? If so, in which language, for how long, and can I do it here?
What is the total tuition for all six years, and can it be raised during my studies?
What language will my clinical placements be in, and what language teaching is built into the programme?
What does Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed say about my specific plan? Ask them directly.
What does Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen say about SU and tuition support for this specific programme?
